title: Prosecuting Comey remains at the center of Trump DOJ’s legal priorities | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

The three attempts to criminally charge formerFBI Director James Comeywere only the beginning.

Over the past week, several government proceedings have shined a light on the outsize reach of the Comey cases that the Justice Department under President Donald Trump has pursued, and how Comey and others close to him still face the threat of more criminal charges.

Two men nominated by Trump to federal judgeships answered questions from the Senate Judiciary Committee about the role each played in one of the Comey cases in North Carolina. In another case in Washington, DC, the Justice Department said late last month it intends to try to indict Comey again. And Comey’s former lawyer Dan Richman publicly accused the Justice Department of a sustained harassment campaign in another Comey-related investigation, which resulted in grand jury activity in Florida and the threat of charges against Richman.

No judge has made a ruling that Comey has been singled out for prosecution unfairly, or vindictively targeted by the Justice Department.

Yet together, the recent efforts keep Comey at the center of the political discourse and the law enforcement agendafor Trump, who fired the FBI director in 2017 and has continued to list him as a top foe.

The Justice Department’s efforts to prosecute Comey for threats, leaks, lying or conspiracy, all relate to different episodes from his service as FBI Director or his time as a private citizen afterward. The Comey cases have repeatedly included sign-off by high-ranking Justice Department officials and kudos from Trump’s White House.

People around Comey say he is anticipating the possibility that the Justice Department asks a grand jury in Washington, DC, to indict him for a felony violation of the Espionage Act – a leak allegation that prosecutors have already levied against Comey on paper in court but is essentially on pause until there is further court activity.

“It would almost be funny if it weren’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice,” Comey said in his most recent public statement responding to the charge, maintaining his innocence.

Prosecutors have accused Comey of sending information to the New York Times in October 2016 that constituted a leak of sensitive government information, but he has yet to be indicted by a grand jury.

“I had about two hours before the grand jury today,” prosecutor Dustin Farahnak said at a hearing in early October, before indicating the Justice Department planned to spend more time on a Comey leak indictment in the following weeks. “To present this case requires, I would believe, much more time. And I had wanted to indict it today. That’s fair. Cards are on the table. I was unable to do so.”

While Farahnak and other DOJ prosecutors could present that indictment for approval any day now, other attorneys connected to a different Comey case — this one on allegations he threatened Trump’s life by sharing a social media post of seashells on the beach last year — are up for promotions to lifetime judicial appointments from Trump.

The Republican-controlled Senate is ushering several Trump appointees through the confirmation process before Democrats can govern with a wide majority in Congress beginning in January.

One of the nominees, Philip Aubart, a North Carolina-based prosecutor, attempted to build a case that Comey’s 2025 Instagram post, which included the photo of seashells spelling out “86 47,”was the same type of violent lingo used by mobsters.

The phrase “86” is sometimes used to describe “nixing,” or removing something, and Trump is the 47th president.

Another of Trump’s current district judge nominees, Brian Meyers, is a magistrate judge in the New Bern, NC, federal courthouse where Comey is being prosecuted for threatening Trump.

Meyers, who’s been a magistrate judge since 2020, said he signed off on search warrants for Comey and his wife’s email accounts as part of the investigation. “That warrant was presented to me. I reviewed it, as is a matter of public record in that case, as it is there’s a redacted version filed in that case with my signature on it. I was the duty magistrate judge presented to that day,” Meyers said at a Senate Judiciary hearing this week. “That is the extent of my involvement.”

A Republican senator contacted Meyers about the federal district judge position a few months later, Durbin noted at the hearing Wednesday.

However, there is no evidence in the public record that Meyers and Aubart were being rewarded for their approvals in the Comey seashell case.

Aubart separately spoke about work for the US Attorney’s office on the case.

“I played a role in that prosecution. I’m no longer playing a role in that prosecution,” Aubart said.

Aubart also said he had been asked to work on the Comey seashell investigation by the US Attorney in eastern North Carolina, despite being in a supervisory role in the office.

About a week after he signed a search warrant application documents for Comey’s electronic data this March, Republican senators’ offices began discussing with him a judicial opening in the Middle District of North Carolina. Comey was charged in North Carolina’s eastern district court in May.

Aubart said that in his interview with the White House Counsel’s Office this fall for the judgeship, he brought up his work on the Comey case. “It came up when I raised it, just as a matter, I think, that would have been of concern to the committee,” Aubart said.

Durbin pointed out Aubart traveled to Phoenix to interview a mobster, Salvatore “Sammy the Bull” Gravano, for the Comey case.

“What did he have to do with seashells?” Durbin asked.

“He was questioned about his knowledge of the use of the term 86,” Aubart said at the hearing on Wednesday.

“You’ve taken an unusually hands-on approach to the Comey prosecution. In April 2026, you and a case agent directed the FBI to conduct keyword searches of trial transcripts from US v. Gambino, a case Comey prosecuted more than 30 years ago,” Durbin also said.

Comey’s indictment is still pending in the federal court in eastern North Carolina for the seashell social media post. A federal judge hasn’t yet ruled on several of Comey’s arguments that the case should be dismissed.

Previously, Comey won the dismissal of a different indictment against him that alleged he lied. A federal judge determined the prosecutor who had secured that charge, Lindsey Halligan, didn’t have the authority to do so. The Justice Department is appealing the dismissal.

Comey’s lawyers argued during a hearing last month in the Washington, DC., leaks case that they believe a harassment campaign is evident.

“The Government has not disavowed possibly using this [charging document] to arrest Mr. Comey,” his defense lawyer, Ephraim McDowell, said in court late last month about the potential case related to leaking national security details. “FBI agents were outside Mr. Comey’s house.

“The Government has had over ten years now to try to prosecute this case,” he added, noting that prior Justice Department prosecutors had looked at the leak case against Comey twice years ago, and decided not to charge him.

The judge, Trevor McFadden of the DC District Court, told a prosecutor in late August Comey doesn’t need to be arrested with law enforcement fanfare at the moment.

“I will tell you, I will be extremely frustrated if there’s some sort of dawn raid or black pajamas turning up outside Mr. Comey’s home,” the judge said.

Farahnak, the prosecutor, responded, “That’s not going to happen, Your Honor. I want to be very clear about that. That is not going to happen.”

A former lawyer and close contact of Comey’s, law professor Daniel Richman, separately said in court filings on Friday that the “harassment campaign” toward Comey extended to him too, with the threat of prosecution this fall in Florida.

Richman has long been tied to Comey as a conduit of information around the time Trump and Comey were publicly at odds, when Trump first became president and Comey was FBI director. Richman also served as his lawyer on some matters, which has become a key issue for investigators looking at possible cases around Comey.

The Florida activity came as part of a possible avenue of the Justice Department targeting Comey and others in a conspiracy investigation Trump has long sought.

The prosecutors’ effort had appeared to fall apart temporarily, over the past several weeks when its lead investigator resigned. Yet this week, a person familiar with that investigation told CNN the Department is sending Bill Essayli, Los Angeles’s top federal prosecutor, to Florida to assist with a criminal investigation tied to the 2022 search of Mar-a-Lago and Jack Smith’s probe of classified documents found at the estate.

The move signals the DOJ is reviving its efforts to investigate a theory of Trump’s that government officials committed crimes in several federal investigative and intelligence efforts dating back to Comey’s era at the FBI and continuing into recent years.

Previously in that investigation, investigators attempted to draw Richman into speaking to the FBI and a grand jury this fall while also potentially looking at charging him criminally, Richman’s lawyers say.

Richman’s lawyers were told in September he was a target in the investigation, and potentially facing an obstruction charge for not directly speaking to FBI.

When the FBI later visited him on August 30, Richman wasn’t there, but one of the agents raised the possibility that his building staff could be charged with obstruction if they weren’t let up to his apartment, according to Richman’s legal team.

Staff of his apartment building who had turned FBI agents away when Richman wasn’t at home, Richman’s lawyers say.

Richman says the FBI’s approach to him appears to have motivated prosecutor Joe DiGenova, who had been leading the “grand conspiracy investigation” until his abrupt resignation in September. DiGenova told Richman’s lawyers he could face possible obstruction charges for attempting to evade the grand jury subpoena this fall, according to Richman’s court filing.

Richman says he ultimately declined to testify by citing his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination when he appeared before the grand jury in Florida in September.

CNN’s Evan Perez, Hannah Rabinowitz and Khariss Bender contributed to this report.
